utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today's business, Mr. Tieger, as you know, Mr. Robinson has informed the Chamber that he would like his motion to exclude Sarajevo evidence to be resolved before the Prosecution case is closed. While the Chamber does not necessarily agree that this matter must be resolved before the Prosecution case is closed, it does see the value in doing so if possible. Thus, the Chamber would like to know how this matter is progressing. You told us last time that the meeting with the Rule 70 provider was going to take place in the week of 17th of April. Did that meeting take place? If necessary, we may go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we move briefly into private session, Mr. President, just out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I shall repeat my question for you. So my question relates to your Croatia binding order motion. You have now conducted two interviews, one with Mr. Tudjman and the other with Mr. Zagorec. The Chamber would like to know what impact in your view this has on your binding order motion, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Having concluded those two interviews, we are in a position to withdraw the motion for binding order because we've been unable to establish that there are records in the possession of the Croatian government that have not been given over to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your oral withdrawal on this matter is final one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if we come up with subsequent information that leads us to believe that they do have records, we might wish to make a second binding order motion, but it's final in the sense that you can take that off your books as far as we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. The Chamber notes that that motion has been withdrawn. Having said that, shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may we have P04995, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, when we left off last week we had just finished speaking about your Sarajevo reports. And now we're going to begin to speak about the Srebrenica reports. Now, the report you see on the screen before you, this is your report from 2009 on Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was your task in writing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was written to provide new evidence on the missing persons from the -- related to the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995 and to provide evidence about identifications of these individuals. As particular class of identifications that we were looking at were DNA-based identifications produced by International Commission for Missing Persons, ICMP, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And this is an older report. This is not the most recent one you've written; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report from 2009, a report that was marking ten years of research into victims of the fall of Srebrenica. It is like, I think, a ninth report in a series that we made. There is a more recent one which is however of a different type than what we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the main source used in writing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report is about missing persons. This is a very special category of victims. These victims cannot be reported in official death notifications, as they are missing. The source that was used for this report is the ICRC list of missing persons, actually I call it a list but it is a number of different lists compiled by ICRC. ICRC is the International Commission for Red Cross, an organisation mandated to collect information about persons going missing in all conflicts all over the world and to trace these individuals in all possible ways to make reports about the fate of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the case of the events at Srebrenica, when was it that ICRC first started taking information?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: ICRC started collecting the reports about missing of individuals directly after the fall of Srebrenica during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were collecting information not only on Srebrenica but on the entire conflict, entire war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Srebrenica was just this major episode, major incident that they were also covering. They published their first edition of the list for Bosnia in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What other main source did you use in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make clear first that the first edition of 1996 is just one of many next editions published by ICRC. So for this report, for 2009 report, we used the edition of 2005 and a separate list of ICRC missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica of October 2008. The second major source used for this report was the ICMP list of DNA identifications of Srebrenica victims, a list that was issued in November 2008. And again, it is a list that has been updated systematically by ICMP and recently we received yet another update, but at that time we had the 2008 November update at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Besides these two sources, did you consult other sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The methodology applied here in this report, for this report, was our standard methodology. That means sources like the 1991 census, voters' registers of 1997, 1998, and 2000 were used as a standard. In addition to these two groups of sources we also used the official registration of internally displaced persons and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 2000. This is a source which we briefly called DDPR. And we also used a number of smaller contextual sources. I want to stress that in order to study the victims of Srebrenica we basically used on one hand ICRC records on the missing persons and on the other hand the ICMP records of DNA identifications. These two were cross-referenced, compared, and through this we were able to conclude how many persons reported missing were as well identified by ICMP, meaning that their bodies were exhumed from mass, entire, graves in the Srebrenica area, their bodies were sampled, I mean remains were -- samples were taken from remains. DNA profiles were made and compared with the profiles of the surviving relatives. So that's the core of our work. All other sources were used for certain important purposes. Like, for instance, the 1991 census was used as a major reference source to validate information about missing persons. Sources on displaced persons and refugees were used to eliminate possible survivors. Voters' registers, 1997, 1998, 2000 with the same purpose, to find and eliminate possible survivors. And smaller contextual sources were used to compare the results obtained from the major sources with those from smaller sources. What I mean contextual, we also used a source -- a smaller source on displacement or on surviving population that became displaced and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excuse me, just for the sake of public there was no -- any translation in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From when did you not hear the translation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Her last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just in case, could you repeat from voters' registers 1997. From there could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you hear the translation of my intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, now I hear but for few sentences, last sentences, I heard only English. And I suppose the public also didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I am repeating my last answer. In that answer I summarised the main sources which we used to study victims of the fall of Srebrenica were on one hand the ICRC list of missing persons and on the other hand the ICMP DNA identifications of Srebrenica victims. We cross-referenced these two in order to draw conclusions about how many individuals reported missing were later found in mass graves and other graves in Srebrenica area and identified through the DNA analysis of human remains and of surviving relatives. Other sources that we used, like for instance 1991 population census and voters' registers of 1997 and 1998 and 2000 were used as a standard -- as part of our standard methodology. The 1991 census to validate information about individuals reported missing, voters' registers, in order to find possible survivors and eliminate them from our list of victims. Other sources, official records of internally displaced persons and refugees and similar were also used with the same purpose, to eliminate possible survivors.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Doctor, now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. At the end of your previous answer you referred to smaller contextual sources. If you could explain it as well, just in case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant in this case we also used additionally a set of databases provided from authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina also on displaced persons and refugees from particularly the Srebrenica area. We used them as additional source, not as the main source, because the main source used was actually far broader and better in terms of quality than this additional one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Dr. Tabeau, I want to now focus on the main sources which you mentioned you cross-referenced for the purposes of this report, and that's the ICMP list and the ICRC list. What was the methodology you used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, are you following the proceedings in the language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, I am following, but I'm having problems related to my health condition due to this ventilation. The air that is being blown onto my head is too strong and too cold and I cannot afford to suffer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like the Registry to look into the matter again. I thought that has been resolved, but -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be resolved. If you have -- are suffering from similar problem, please let us know. In the meantime, we can continue. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The methodology that you used, was this the same methodology you used for your other reports?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same standard methodology, matching of sources the individual record level which simply means that we trace individuals between the lists we use in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we already spoke about that methodology last week and I'd now like to look at the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 23719, and this is the handout that was given out last week, and specifically I'm looking at page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's on the very top we have table 1. Can you tell us about this table.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a table summarising our update of the previous OTP list of Srebrenica missing. The previous list is mentioned in this table as 2005 OTP list. On the top of this list there is a second category called 2008 ICRC list, for which we only see 29 additional cases not reported in our 2005 list. So what is shown here is how we critically looked at what we have done previously and expanded this result by using one more additional list of ICRC missing persons from Srebrenica. This second list is mentioned as the 2008 list and relates exclusively to Srebrenica victims, exactly the same as 2005 list. So the overall total of missing persons on the 2009 OTP list of Srebrenica missing is 7.692. That is the first type of information included in table 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the second column of information that's labelled "number of identified," does this refer to the ICMP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to DNA identifications, positive identifications of course, of persons reported at the same time as missing individuals by ICRC. So we cross-referenced it to, linked the records representing the same individuals, and are able to say how many of those reported missing at the same time have been identified by ICMP. So the overall total of positive DNA identifications out of 7.692 was by 2009 5.061, which accounted for 65.8 per cent of the OTP list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, if you move --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was waiting for the French translation. I wonder if Dr. Tabeau has explained to us the meaning of an OTP list. I may have missed it. How does it differ from ICRC report or something like that? Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, can you talk about that, the difference between the OTP list and the ICRC list, if there's any difference at all.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICRC list, the core list that was used for the OTP list, is a broad list for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, and obviously the entire war period. It is not what we need for the victims of the fall of Srebrenica. So using this core list as the basis for our work, we extracted relevant records using two criteria. First of all, the place criterion and second time criterion. Places considered to be relevant to the fall of Srebrenica comprised Srebrenica municipality itself and a number of other municipalities in this area, in total ten municipalities, which is all discussed in the annex, I think first annex, to 2009 OTP report. Time, of course, was also an important criterion. The persons who went missing in July 1995 and also later in the months between August and until December 1995 were also considered relevant. But as we will see in few minutes there is a very clear time distribution of disappearances that tells us that most of them occurred in July 1995. So it is all discussed in first annex to the 2009 report. So the 2005 OTP list or 2009 OTP list only means that we talk about a selection of ICRC records relevant to the fall of Srebrenica and not about the entire complete list for Bosnia and entire war period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you had mentioned earlier that there was a 65 per cent overlap when you did your comparison, and we can see that on table 1; but can you now move down to table 12 and tell us how that table is connected.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a table that is much more complex than the first one. It is much more complex first because it shows the result produced by myself and my team since the year 2000 up to 2009, but I suggest we focus right now on the last row in this table that is related to the results reported in the 2009 report. And the second reason for the complexity of this table is that we go beyond the overlap of ICRC records and ICMP records, and in this table we show as well how many non-overlapping records were reported by ICMP as positive DNA identifications of Srebrenica victims. So if we go to the first column of this table in the last row we see the familiar number, 7.692, it is what we just discussed, the same number from table 1. Next to it there is a column called "Srebrenica identified (ICMP)." This is a separate information summarising the progress ICMP made in DNA identifications completely independently from the OTP efforts, our efforts, to quantify the victims of Srebrenica. So by 2009, or rather, as based on November 2008, ICMP update in total they reported 5.555 positive identifications of Srebrenica victims. It's a large number and in the third column we again show how many of these 5.555 overlapped with the OTP missing persons. So this number also familiar, we just discussed it in table 1, is 5.061. That's the overlap of two independent sources reported -- reporting on Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, yes, I have to admit this is rather complex. Still, we see the table 1 in this monitor. We see the "familiar" number 7.692 here, but there number of identified is 5.061, but in table 12 you said identified numbers are 5.555 and 5.061 is the number of overlap. I have difficulty in following that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ICMP works completely independently from the OTP, from ICRC, from anybody. So once a while they issue a list of DNA identifications of Srebrenica victims. This list issued at the end of 2008 included 5.555 cases, persons. This is a list that can be compared with all kinds of sources. We compared this list with our list of missing persons from Srebrenica, from the fall of Srebrenica. If you compare, you can see how many cases are identical, the same on both lists, but you will also see that there are unique parts to the sources compared. So the unique part in ICMP records obviously was there as the overlap identified is lower than 5.555. It is not that we -- yeah, it is just, you know, an exercise, you know, that we take independent sources compiled by completely different groups and we did do it on purpose because there is a lot of uncertainty in measuring or reporting victims of war, and we want to make sure that all those who will be on our list are also confirmed by other sources, by the ICMP in this case. And obviously next to 5.061 there are other categories in this table. And if we go, for instance, to the column called "new victims," identified persons, new victims, this is one part of this unique part of ICMP, this unique part of ICMP, that is not reported on our list of missing persons. So they have extra 213 cases that we were unable to put on our list because ICRC didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- a graphical example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should bear in mind the interval between the English and French translation. We should put a pause. If you see the number 5.555, which is Srebrenica identified, so those parts that are not overlapping overlapped with the next number which is 5.061. So those, about 500, are already identified. Are they not new victims, all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all of them, not all of them for a simple reason that there is this matching process between ICRC records and ICMP records. For a group of records, 213, we are sure we cannot match them, we cannot see any similar cases or the same cases on our list. But there is another category excluded overlap which actually relates to less certain matches. So we have made some matches but we are uncertain about how well they represent our victims between these two lists. So we actually excluded them all together from the analysis because there is uncertainty there and we leave this group for later. Perhaps there will be more results that will help us improve our matching in a later time. But for now we know for sure that 213 are new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think I now understand the mathematics. So to put it -- I may put it like this. Please correct me if I'm wrong. 5.555 minus 5.061 equals 281 plus 213?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could explain to us again when this overlap is to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Overlap is excluded if we are not convinced that our matches are true matches, that they make it possible to say that two records, one from ICRC, one from ICMP, describe the same individual. There is a certain degree of similarity in these two compared records, but we cannot declare that this is highly reliable and highly likely that this is one and the same case. So we just exclude them for now, but with time we expect there will be better information about these cases that perhaps will make it possible for us to report them as true matches. This kind of matching issue can be better understood if we think of ICMP records with multiple names, first names, like, you know, if brothers were killed or sons and father, sometimes they are reported jointly in one record and this record has three different names. In such cases ICMP does not include at some stages date of birth of these victims, and for us it is important to have the information about the date of birth, or at least year of birth, in order to declare matches as good matches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does your report -- part of your report, main report, deal with this matching exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there is an annex which actually discusses quite a degree of detail of our matching methodology in the context of ICMP records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may look for the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, if you could be kind enough to show us an example how that matching exercise is being done in terms of this excluded, overlap, and new victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Just for the record, this is explained in annex 6.6 and that is page 102 of this particular report; that's the matching part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Third page from the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, when we look at the actual Excel spreadsheet we can give you an example of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that will happen in one moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But, Dr. Tabeau, just to stay on this table so we can get to that spreadsheet, I want to focus on the number 7905. Please tell us what that number represents.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number we can find in the last row in the column called "Accepted victims (integrated)." This is a third-last column. It is an important column because it integrates two numbers. One is the number of missing persons plus the number of new victims identified based on ICMP identifications. This is the number 213 reported in table 12 which we just discussed. So these two numbers, 7.692 plus 213 new victims gives 7.905, and this is the new overall total of Srebrenica victims on the 2009 OTP list.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you gave that number back in your 2009 report, at the time was ICMP giving you information that joined Srebrenica victims with Zepa victims?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this number represents both Srebrenica and Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It's mainly Srebrenica, though, because for Zepa the number at that time, as far as I remember, was 103 victims -- well, generally Zepa is a totally different scale than Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And when we talk about your most recent results we'll separate them as well. But if you just look down to figure 1 you spoke earlier about time of disappearance. Tell us about this chart.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This chart is showing the distribution of going missing by calendar month in 1995. The date of disappearance is reported by ICRC. It is just one of the two major items, one is date of disappearance, one is place of disappearance. So from this chart, figure 1, we see that a vast majority of victims disappeared in July 1995, as of course expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the source of this information is ICRC; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can turn the page of the handout --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can you go back to table 12. What does the excluded potential survivors number mean? Does it have any impact on accepted victims number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, of course not. The excluded potential survivors are excluded and are not granted in the numbers reported under accepted victims integrated. They are shown here to summarise our efforts related to our searching for potential survivors. We found a number of such records, studied them, cross-reference in several sources like, you know, starting with the census, further voters register 1997, 1998, and 2000, records of displaced persons and refugees, and based on this analysis these 12 are excluded. Once ICRC reports a very small cases alive. So that means exclusions. So one of these cases excluded is just this kind of ICRC alive person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to understand it correctly, does this 12 -- I'm sorry, I correct. Is this 12 included in Srebrenica missing number, i.e., 7.692?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not. It's not included in any list of victims. This is just a separate category, separate category not included in Srebrenica missing, not included in new victims, not included in accepted victims, not included in ICMP identifications. It is just excluded. It's not there. Only exists as this separate number. In the list that is attached with the 2009 report these 12 victims are reported in a separate annex as exclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then was this 12 included in the original ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At some point they were but not -- you know, ICRC basically produces a list not only for Srebrenica but also for the -- for other episodes. Anyway, they were included but now we identified some overlap with sources on survivors and they are excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was wondering if this number has nothing to do with this Srebrenica missing, why this appears on this table at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, did you put this number here to show that you, OTP demographic unit, has done ongoing work with contextual sources to exclude any survivors?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is to address these activities in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we were just talking about time of disappearance, figure 1. If we turn the page the next page in e-court we look at figure 3. Does this regard place of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Figure 3 reports on the place of disappearance. This figure shows a selection of places, the largest places reported as the place of disappearance. It's rather a clear picture. A few places, like five places, including Potocari, forest, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, and Kamenica, these five places alone are responsible for a very large percentage of disappearances. As a matter of fact, actually it is only five municipalities where almost all these references can be located. These places here in figure 3 are smaller than municipalities. They are concrete places, like Potocari such a place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 11435 -- excuse me, it has a P number already, P04996. And if we can have e-court page 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, attached to your report itself, did you also include the list of names themselves?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a long list of names attached with this report. What I'm seeing on the screen actually is the first page of introduction to this list. This page explains the six components of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And you had just mentioned when we were talking about that excluded number of 12, excluded potential survivors, and we see on the screen before us the parts, do those 12 people, are they listed in one of these parts?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is part 5 which is the list of exclusions, 12 cases reported in table 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, if we looked at this in hard copy, this actual appendix is quite thick so we're not going to go through it, but can you tell us within these parts do you have an actual listing of the names that are on your missing list, missing persons list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is listed here in parts 1, 2, 3, which are the major components of our list. Part 1 is the records that enter our 2009 list from the previous, 2005 OTP list. Part 2 are additional ICRC records, the 29 that we discussed in the beginning of today. Part 3 are the new names of victims, the 213 names that we identified from the ICMP records. Part 4 are less likely matches, uncertain matches. These are the 218 which we don't count in our statistics as victims. Part 5 are exclusions that we don't count in our statistics on Srebrenica victims. And part 6 are cancelled records of cases alive coming from ICRC as a source. So it is a very long list of almost 8.000 names that is attached in this annex. We list them using first name, father's name, surname, date of birth, or just year of birth. For ICRC records we are able to tell exactly the date of disappearance, the place of disappearance. And for those cases that have been matched with the ICMP records, we are able to insert additional information about the protocol number of this victim, the protocol number meaning the reference number of this victim identification report, and the name of site where the remains were exhumed from.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. In your explanation you mentioned 218 which we don't count in our statistics as victims. In fact, did you mean 281?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the report -- the updated report for the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 23710, please. Mr. President, for this report we will go through the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you recently came to the OTP a few weeks ago, and when you came what was your task?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task was to study the latest update of ICMP on Srebrenica identified persons and cross-reference this update with the OTP records of missing persons and assess the overlap between these two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: To assess that overlap, did you use the matching approach?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The methodology used in cross-referencing was exactly the same as I have always used for these demographic reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're now going to move to Sanction to show the spreadsheet and I would ask that this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand the decision from last week in regard to the ICMP material. That information is included here. So for the time being I ask that this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one is from Srebrenica that we can see from the name of this particular sheet at the bottom.

utterances.text: Now, on this spreadsheet the Trial Chamber sees two new columns that were not on the original ICMP spreadsheet and that's column O and P. Under O it says B-A-Z, BAZ (OTP 2009) integrated and then 2009 new & less certain integrated. Did you add this information to the spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

Having this number makes it possible to search through the ICRC lists, any list ever published, and check information about this particular person, on the circumstances and time of his or her disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the BAZ number, is that just the ICRC identification number just as protocol ID number is the ID number for ICMP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So any time the Trial Chamber sees that column filled in, does that mean that there's a match between ICRC and ICMP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now going back to the President's question in regard to how you made the match, can you tell us, can you walk us through that process by looking through this spreadsheet and I'll go back to the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

I want to draw Your Honours' attention to one thing. We are searching in a very limited environment in this particular case. What I mean by the limited environment is that on one hand there is this detailed list of people selected from ICRC records of whom we know that they were reported as missing as Srebrenica victims and here is another limited environment. This is the Srebrenica victims that is reported -- that are reported by ICMP. So having these two -- these two limited environments if we compared them, if there is a person born on the same or very close date because there are mistakes in that dates with the same names, although there might be differences in the spelling, it is a highly probable match that this is the same person represented in both sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we go back to your column, every time -- under O every time we see that BAZ number have you done a matching process and come up with a link?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So in case of no match with ICRC, there is still a possibility that a victim was included in the 2009 OTP list. utterances.speaker: MS. WEST

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the third line, but record number 2 --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So I've just clicked on the Zepa tab. This regards the list for Zepa victims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- these are also new categories introduced not too long ago but by ICMP. They simply started reporting some exclusions or inconclusive cases. It has rather to do with the information that ICMP teams collected from the family members of these victims during the process of collecting blood samples. There are a few cases of exclusions, I think in total nine cases and some more separately inconclusive cases, but it is always thought that the rationale for declaring a case an exclusion or an inconclusive case relates to this extra information obtained from the relatives of the victims. Well, if we go again to the top to the column R, to keep the column R, yes, then in the ICMP comment there is a case of two brothers, one missing from 1992, another from 1995. If we go to the left then we will see that this is a record with two first names. It is two men reported jointly under this protocol number. As it is often thought that ICMP cannot distinguish on the basis of the DNA profile between the two brothers, they don't know who is who, but they do know from the relatives that one went missing in 1992, another in 1995. But what I can do in such situation, I can search for both brothers and I can check which of the two is included as a Srebrenica missing person and I can search for the other brother and I can make sure that the other brother is not included in the ICRC missing persons. This is what I did in this case and obviously we have a record of the right brother on our list and not of the wrong brother. So if we create a link between the right brother and this particular record we still counted this person only one time, no more than just this one time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So is it fair to suggest that these exclusions and inconclusive cases are ones that you specifically did some work on to make sure they were correctly included or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now I'd like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is a PIP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

Now they are funded also by the government, and are mandated to work on their identification of Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go to the results. If we can go back to the handout to the last page, page 19. 65 ter 23719, page 19. utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same table, only now it has been expanded. It has two additional columns at the right side. The second-last is called number of identified 2012 and the last column is per cent of the overlap between the 2012 update and the OTP list from 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can just do that in reverse. We see on the bottom line 7692 and then 5061. Those are from our earlier table; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the new number you just gave, 6241, is this the updated number for the most recent ICMP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This number is the -- coming from 2012 ICMP update. The number 6.241 is the overlap of this latest update of ICMP with the number 7.692. It used to be much lower. It used to be 5.061 as of 2009 report. Now it is 6.241, which gives us an overlap of 81.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for those 6.241 records were lines that we would see on the spreadsheet if we looked at it. For each of those records would there be a box filled in with a BAZ number or with a previous ICMP number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there would be such a box and in particular it would be the BAZ box available for every of these 6.241.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can move below this to the next table, table 12, again this is familiar. But I want to go to the second-to-last column, new victims identified 2012. And we see a number there, 116. What is that number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the victims that I was unable to confirm on any component of the 2009 list of Srebrenica victims, and therefore they are listed here as additional new cases from the 2012 update.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this similar to what you did in 2009, where we see the column labelled new victims identified 2009 and you came up with 213?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So to get to the last column, 8.021 --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- what numbers do you have to consider?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to obtain this number we have to take 7.905 previously accepted Srebrenica victims, once again 7.905, and on the top of it I am taking the 116 new cases from 2012. And the result is 8.021 records representing both Srebrenica and Zepa victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know how many of the 2012 ICMP records regard Zepa? Strike that. Let me ask you another question. If we take this number 8.021 you just said it includes Srebrenica and Zepa. If you subtract the Zepa cases, what's the number for just Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number for Srebrenica, I think from this number we would have to subtract 116 cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coincidentally -- well, it's the same number as new cases, but it is not the total new cases -- Zepa cases. Well, once again, 8.021, 8.021, is the new overall number of Srebrenica victims and Zepa victims jointly, obtained from the integration of the latest ICMP update from 2012 with the previously obtained number, which was 7.905. These 8.021 cases covers both, Srebrenica, the fall of Srebrenica, and the fall of Zepa. Zepa is a small incident compared with Srebrenica. In these 8.021 cases there are only 116 cases that are related to Zepa. It is consistent with the ICRC reports on the missing persons from Zepa. utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the 2012 report, which is 65 ter 23710. And I'd also like to tender the associated spreadsheet, and I would like that to be under seal for the time being, 65 ter 23712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we do that, one further question about new victims 2012, Dr. Tabeau. You told us that they are the victims that you were not able to confirm on any component of the 2009 list of Srebrenica victims. I don't think I understood that part. Where did that come from at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These new cases come from the ICMP update of January this year. As previously, this update has been compared by myself with the previous OTP list and the previous ICMP update. So I identified a number of cases that are not included previously at all, not in the previous ICMP data, not in the ICRC used for the OTP list. It is just like new victims, which can be understood perhaps more easily if we think about how is it possible that ICMP can report on new victims different from ICRC reports. Yes, it is possible. It is that the reports each of these organisations obtains goes -- is from the actual families of the victims. Some families contacted both ICRC and ICMP. In the case of ICMP they even donated blood for the identification. Some of them, however, a small number would go exclusively to ICRC and some of them would go exclusively to ICMP. So if we think of how is it possible that, you know, there is still this new category, new records reported by ICMP, the answer is: Yes, it is possible. It is possible. Which relates to the way these organisations operate and how in -- for months provide information to each of these organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So originally these 116 people were not included in the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections to the admission of these two reports, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them both. Putting the latter one, the spreadsheet, under seal provisionally. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 23710 will be Exhibit P5004. 65 ter 23712 will be Exhibit P5005 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm changing subject matters at the moment. Is this the time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, on Thursday you discussed a statistical formula, it was the capture recap -- is that working?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's working now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we were discussing the capture/recapture formula, which was a formula to estimate the overall size of a population when you couldn't actually count individual people. You were asked by the Trial Chamber if you could come up with a more simplified form of the formula to make it more digestible. Have you been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this I need to use ELMO. I prepared an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am using an example of ducks which is because first applications of this method were made among others for ducks. Actually in 1930 there was an interesting paper published for ducks. So ducks is an example of a wide population. We don't know exactly how many are there. Sometimes we have the impression that there are very many because they are extremely, extreme noisy. And in order to know more about how many are there outside in a park or in a natural area it is possible to make an experiment which is designed to provide the unknown size of the population of ducks. I have on ELMO an example in which we see three circles. The biggest one is white inside and represents the entire population of ducks living in a park. This is what is unknown, how many, and this is what we need to know. In order to estimate this unknown number we take two samples from the population, two samples of ducks. The first one is the yellow one. The yellow represents the first sample. There are 200 ducks selected. Every single of the 200 gets a tag on her leg so they are all marked. All 200 have a tag that we can follow later and we let them go back to the wild. So the proportion of the yellow circle to the big white circle is the first one that we need to keep in mind. The sample size of the first sample, yellow circle to the big white circle, that is one proportion we have to think of. So sometime later we take another sample of ducks, this is the green circle. The green circle comprises 150 ducks. When we catch them we check whether they have this tag or not. For a number of them we saw that, yes, there were 30 of them with this tag. The proportion of the tag ducks that is represented in my drawing with the light green colour to the entire sample -- second sample, which is 150 ducks, is the second one that we need to remember. The assumption of this method is that these two proportions are equal, are the same. That means the yellow circle to the big white one is the same as the proportion of the 30 tagged ducks to 150 selected in the second sample. It's just a simple equality of two proportions that are used to draw the formula, which is given below. So N1 is the first sample, N2 is the second sample, N12 is the overlap of the two samples, is the overlap of the two samples. If we make these two proportions N1 divided by N and we say it is equal to the proportion calculated as N12 divided by N2, these two proportions give us the formula at the bottom, which I will write down perhaps the two proportions in order to make it more explicit. The first proportion, yellow circle, N1 divided by the big white circle, divided by N, equals the light green area of the green circle divided by the size of the entire green circle. After a simple change, transformation of this equality, we obtain this formula, from which we can calculate the unknown size of the population of ducks, which is in this particular case 1.000. There is also another rationale behind this method. This other rationale originates from the probability theory. In the blue box here I'm showing a very, very old formula for the probabilities of independent events, event A and event B. So the probability of a joint occurrence of two events, A and B, according to this formula, equals probability of the first event, A times probability of the event B. So the A and B events are nothing different but these two samples, yellow and green circles on my drawing. And the probability of the joint occurrence of the event A and B is an overlap of the two sources -- two samples. It is the light green area on the drawing. And under the formula I just put the numbers to express the probabilities. And after again a transformation of the numbers we end with exactly the same formula for the unknown N, as previously discussed. There is one important assumption to this method. There are few more but one is really very fundamental. The two samples are independent, which in case of the sources that were used in the Sarajevo reports, one source being the Bakije funeral home and the second source being the Sarajevo household survey, we can with confidence conclude that these two sources were statistically independent because reporting a victim in one source did not change the chance of the same victim being reported in the second source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you give me an example of sample in this case. First N1 in this case, yellow ducks, could you give me an example of such sample. This is not the whole ducks living in the park.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But could you give me some example to concretely understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So in order to create such a sample a person would have to go and catch the ducks one by one to end with 200 ducks in the sample. Having caught all these ducks, 200, we know for sure that this isn't the complete population of ducks because there are many, many more of course. So that is how the sample was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having caught these ducks from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a natural environment like a large park we can think of, for instance, The Hague with all its parks as the environment from which we will caught the ducks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are doing this exercise in order to know the number of total ducks that are living in the park?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So a certain individual went to a park and caught every duck that were in the park at that point of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if it would be all ducks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All ducks, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in that park it wouldn't be a sample. It would be perhaps a sample but representing a larger environment than just this park, right. So the wide population we have to, of course, be specific about what is the wide population that we are approximating or estimating, you know, the size of. In this particular example I am saying a park, what is this park, whether it is just one park in The Hague like, I don't know, Rosarium, for instance, park. Rosarium park is just one of the parks in The Hague but there are more parks in The Hague that this area is kind of -- you can even work, you know, these green parts will take you from one park to the next. So it is not just this park that this population of ducks is living in. They will be living in all parks in the neighbourhood. This would be the natural habitat for these ducks, and in order to know how many are there in this natural habitat we have to estimate because we are unable to go and to catch every single duck living there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If you could further expand on the concrete example, green sample, that means there would be another park.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, this was my mistake. So the second sample is a second measurement. So, as Your Honour noted, at some point in time we go and take the first sample and then we put them back and let them mix again with the remaining ducks. So we wait some time and we go again. We can go to exactly same place. So from the same environment we pick another sample and it is justified to expect that we will end with a different sample, largely different, not entirely different though. There will be this overlap, light green area which is marked here. And the same, you know, it is a very good illustration of the relationships between sources on victims. Sources on victims are very different from regular statistical sources like the population census. Population census would represent the white circle here, right. It would be all of the people. But because of war the statistical system is most likely not operating the usual way. We don't have all reports on what time deaths and especially about victims like missing persons of whom we don't have death certificates at the time they were gone missing. So we have samples. We have several samples, samples that often largely overlap. But there will be also this unique part in every sample. In this particular case the light green area is the core, the overlap, and the dark green is the unique part to the second sample. And the yellow part, non-overlapping part of the first sample is the unique part of the first sample. This is quite a normal situation in the analysis of victims of conflict. This is why it is very important to analyse more sources than just one and check the overlap and check how many are in the core, in the overlap, and how many victims are in the unique parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I take it then, Mr. Karadzic, will be asking you many questions about the applicability of this principle to the victims. Mr. Karadzic, to understand you correct, although I note the absence of your expert, Dr. Pasalic, are you challenging this principle itself, capture and recapture principle in statistics field?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I'm going to demonstrate why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Doctor, before Ms. West proceeds, let me thank you very much indeed for simplifying the situation, making it more digestible and the ducks. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With pleasure. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, the other day there was the discussion about - you were present for it - about certain items that had been disclosed and one of the items that Mr. President asked about was your list, your flagged list, of the 1991 census of those people who became displaced. That flagged list, is it your practice to disclose the results of the steps you took along the way? In other words, did you disclose that list to the Prosecutors to hand over?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the practice in cases like this one is, first of all, to provide all the sources that have been analysed in my reports and provide reports discussing -- that are discussing the results. In addition to this, there is the practice of providing extensive annexes in which details of the methodology are disclosed as well. In addition, there are references in terms of published books, articles, where the same methodology is described. I think I am sure that also in this case this practice has been followed, and I am sure I remember myself certain dead-lines from the time I worked in the OTP for disclosing this element I just mentioned. And it was, for instance, for reports. I had a dead-line in May 2009, early May 2009, to submit all the reports that are now presented in this case. And at the same time I am sure that Mr. Karadzic received copies of everything. It's been a long, long time that all these necessary materials were provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, in answer to your question the other day as to whether the flagged list was disclosed, the answer to that is no it was not. However, both sources were disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, there are four addendums to the Galic report that have not been admitted. I've spoken to Mr. Robinson and the Registrar has those numbers. Mr. Robinson has no objection and I would ask -- I would tender those four addendums as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The first one is 65 ter 23695; second, 23696; the next, 23697; and the last is 23698.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, we have no objection, but I hope you won't use that against us when Dr. Karadzic is asking for a little bit more time because we are saving the Prosecution some time in direct examination by doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will all be admitted. Let's give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Very well they will be admitted as Exhibits P5006 through P5009 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Lastly, Your Honour, I would tender the handout which is 23719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it may be convenient to follow the proceedings. Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P5010.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And also, Mr. President, may the Prosecution upload the diagram the doctor had presented in the last explanation and tender that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With Doctor's notation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once again I would like to express my gratitude to you for having met with the Defence team and I am sure it will be helpful in reaching a better understanding. I am also thankful for your thorough approach in explaining the statistics to all the parties to these proceedings. On my part I am going to do my best to put questions to you that can be answered with either a yes or no, and of course you are at liberty to choose which answer you're going to give me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have the last document put on the ELMO once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, am I right if I say that this relates, these samples and their interrelations, pertain to the park which is the largest ellipsis of the three?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this park a contained or a closed system without any entry or exit points?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for this particular population of ducks, they can move but they would remain within the area studied as there wouldn't be birth and migration out of the area or deaths. The measurements were actually made closely one after another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But still within the confines of this particular park?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the result be affected in any way whatsoever if the ducks were to move to another closed system, another park, which was not the subject of investigation and vice versa, if other ducks would migrate to this park?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they moved to another environment, it of course will affect the estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me not even ask you about the love life of the ducks. What if those ducks were to get drunk, to start killing each other, would that have any impact at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it would have an impact on the ducks, but I mean a drunk duck or a dead duck is not alive and healthy duck. But it seems to me that what we should be concentrating on is the mathematical principles and not the mating or drinking habits of ducks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, let me remind you that when talking about Freud you spoke about the love life of eels and the principle is the same, is it not? They're just nuances that have to be altered. Can this be applied to human population in view of the fact that hazardous behaviour like drinking or murders or killing each other, and so on and so forth, are things that are quite common among people unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may answer this. Now, first of all, Sarajevo, the area studied in the two Sarajevo reports, where the estimation was done also using capture/recapture, it was the closed population. That is very important observation that actually makes it possible to apply this method. It is a closed population in the sense that Sarajevo was blocked for long time and it was not possible for the population to cross the front lines to go out and to come back whenever they wanted. So the population that we studied is a closed population, and this is the population that was questioned in order to provide reports about the victims in the Sarajevo households there. Bakije operated within the same closed area and again collected reports on victims from dead population within the front lines, the population that was exposed to risk of being killed. Moreover, those who reported actually were the survivors and they were household heads who actually had a good overview of all what happened to these families during the conflict and during the time the Sarajevo population was closed from the outside world by the front lines. So from this point of view it is actually the assumptions of this method are very well satisfied and I'm not worried about moving, migration, these kind of things because these are not the sources that can give bias to the capture/recapture estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still talking about the principles of the methodology, and what about this situation? What if there were a tunnel between this park and another park and what if there -- the tunnel were used by thousands of ducks who were crossing from one park to the next? Would that be something worth knowing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a tunnel in Sarajevo, we all know that, and it was used to provide aid to the people living in the city from the airport where the aid was delivered. Well, I'm not aware of huge, massive migration through the tunnel out of Sarajevo, or, even more impossible, into the Sarajevo that was under siege and attacked by shelling and snipers. So I don't think it is a realistic scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, Dr. Tabeau. Are you saying that food arrived in Sarajevo through the tunnel from the city airport? Is that what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said there was a tunnel in Sarajevo connecting the part of the city under siege with the Sarajevo airport. What was transported via the tunnel I am not aware in detail because I cannot be. I wasn't there and I wasn't taking reports and I wasn't studying this part of the siege. So the tunnel was there is a very well-known fact. It has been reported by media very frequently. Even recently by BBC there is a wonderful report about Sarajevo also about the tunnel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wouldn't say that it was you who are to blame, but it would be your hosts in Sarajevo who did not inform you about the fact that the aid for Sarajevo passed through the Serbian territory, through the streets, and that tunnel was under Sarajevo and that it connected Hrasnica and Sarajevo and that you could easily enter Sarajevo or leave Sarajevo and people indeed did that as much as they wanted to. So there was a connection between the two, but let's leave that aside and move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move to strike all of that. It's a statement. She already made a comment that she's not the person to talk about what's coming in and out, and this is just a statement without any question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I have a question. If it is correct what I'm saying, would you say that Sarajevo or the largest circle was as closed as you assumed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the population couldn't move freely across the front line and go to the rest of the country and back any time they wanted. I am aware of it, but I didn't study it in my report. So if you need evidence on the population movement in this period in this area, then I'm afraid it's not my reports that can provide you with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another subquestion. On Thursday you mentioned that you had visited the front lines in Sarajevo. When was that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see two positions along the front lines, the Serbian position on one side and the Muslim position on the other side? Did you see two parallel trenches running parallel to each other?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, you know, in 2001 around that time I couldn't see trenches and parallel trenches. It was long after the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, if that was once a confrontation line, what were the parties to that confrontation? There must have been ones on one side and the others on the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are always parties to any confrontation, but I thought that I'm here to speak about statistics and victims and not about parties to conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Tabeau, on Thursday you said that the Serbs had been on hilltops from which they had a good view and they could shoot from there. However, if you had indeed visited the confrontation lines along the hilltops and if you could see that there was 10, 20, or 50 metres between the trenches, then I would suggest that the Muslims were on the same hilltops; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's put it clear. I am not a military expert and I would not comment on the trenches and positions of the armies. It was -- it is not my area simply, you know. It is -- I might have said that the Serbs were there on the hilltops. That is a very well-known fact and I don't think I am making, you know, a discovery here, but that's all I can say. My goal, my objective and task, was to provide statistics on victims. And moreover, I think when making my statistics I clearly distinguished between civilian victims and military victims. So it is not that I'm saying that there were no military victims and that only exclusively civilians were killed. There were both, civilian and military victims. It is all in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Should I be dealing with the matters that you mentioned and that would fall under the category of explanations for your statistical calculations in interpretations thereof and if that is taken into account then I have to deal with that. But if you were only dealing with figures and somebody else should be dealing with implications then I will abandon that topic. But we will come to that. Let me go on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably on Friday to my question you answered this way -- let me put it this way. I posed a question about your conclusion about the deliberate targeting of the civilians, and I asked you: "Does the location of the army have any impact or effect on such result if the -- for example, if an army is located in the middle of civilian population. Does it have any effect on that, Doctor?" And in the course of answering the question, you said: "I believe it does matter where the army is located ... yes. For shelling there is a separate analysis in the report and I compared the victims of shelling for both civilians and soldiers, and the conclusion is not different for this particular category. So these are two different patterns, I think. As for the location of the army, the VRS was located, of course, on the hills with an excellent view on the town down the valley, so I think it was a perfect location for shelling of any victim." Probably, Mr. Karadzic has in mind in posing those questions whether such location has any impact upon your conclusion. Any observations, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand, of course, for everything I said last week and what Your Honour just quoted. And, well, what I tried to say is I am not a military expert to comment on the position of the armies, parties to this conflict. That is one thing. The fact that the VRS army was located on the hills is a very well-known fact that I am sure also in this case has been or will be or, I don't know, is discussed I believe by military experts. So in my view in my report what I am trying to do, I didn't study the armies, their positions and their activities. I studied information on victims, on their causes of death, and on the patterns -- of the patterns of killings for both civilians and military victims. I compared the patterns and I draw conclusions as to whether these patterns were similar and proportional or not. And based on the study of the patterns and causes of death my conclusion is that civilians most likely were targeted and there had to be a different force, a different mechanism, that was killing civilians and soldiers during the siege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have to deal with your conclusions then, but let's complete our duck topic. Would it be better if 200 were recaptured, for example, and then to see what the overlapping was or does it make any difference at all? Can you just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the numbers can change. It is not -- that the numbers I gave in the example are once and forever. It does matter what is the overlap and what are the unique parts, what are the sample sizes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You provided an example here and you gave us the months of March and April as temporal boundaries. Is it significant at all? Is there a constant leading to the exact results when time intervals are longer? Would the time interval be significant at all when we are talking about capture and recapture?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the March and April from the example were given to stress that this is a separate moment at which these two samples were taken. In case of Sarajevo reports, one of the sources, Bakije funeral home, was completed over a number of years starting in April 1992 and continuing in the course of war and the other one was a one-time survey. It was, however, retrospective survey that was meant to collect information about all cases of killings and wounding since the beginning of the siege until the moment of the survey. So I don't think that the March and April from my example do play any role in my actual work. In my view these two sources that are used in the Sarajevo reports both describe the same population and there is nothing that could -- could be spoken up for one source being completely different and uncomparable with the first source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would the result be different, for example, if we take the Sarajevo population and if the capture and recapture period were six months, a year, two years, or even three years? How would that reflect on the Sarajevo population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I want to explain there is nothing like capture/recapture period. It is just the samples that I used for the capture/recapture estimation. What matters is what is the coverage of the samples, whether they are comparable and can be cross-referenced, and my answer is yes they are comparable, they can be cross-referenced, the overlap can be identified, and the assumptions needed for this method are fulfilled. This is why I used these samples in the capture/recapture estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. This will not be counted as your time, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. West, with the assistance of Dr. Tabeau, could you show us the page in her report that applies to capture/recapture to the Sarajevo population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Annex 6.6, I'll give you the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we upload that item.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This would be in e-court -- this would be 65 ter 12130. E-court page is probably 58.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page. Table A6.1 is what we should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This estimation is only made for the period from 1st of April, 1992, to the 9 September 1992. That's the Karadzic Sarajevo report. In order to make this estimation records were extracted from each source relevant only to this period. We have Sarajevo household survey 1.707 cases of Muslims both killed in natural deaths. And then we haves move to Bakije and there is 1.576 cases of both again killed and natural deaths of Muslims. These two sources, samples, are 100 per cent comparable. One was collected at mid-1994 backwards which was retrospectively collecting all information about persons killed or natural death during the siege. And the same is with Bakije.
